doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: San Diego and the state of jazz
title: Concert halls versus noisy night clubs
summary: He thinks the quiet concert hall can be deadly and that great moments often happen in noisy clubs, though jazz will need more concerts.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Do you think putting jazz in the concert hall has been a good thing for the music? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

That’s a great question. Here again, I disagree with a lot of my peers and think that it’s the ideal environment, the concert hall I mean. People are quiet, no cash register noise, no peripheral distractions. But those are the very things that I grew up with, and to me some of the best music happens in those very environments, in clubs where it may be noisy, people talking and laughing, and noise going on behind the bar and sometimes the most creative moments happen in those environs. And a concert hall can be deadly, you know? Not always, but I mean it can be. We’ve all experienced that. So ideally I’d love to see it all coexist. I’d love to see a healthy night club scene and concert outlets for — at least for a certain amount of activity, but I think it’s going to have to be more and more concerts and the universities help there a lot I think, and it’s certainly not happening on T.V., we know that, and anyway, yeah. But I have real mixed emotions. I don’t always think those absolutely quiet, attentive situations are the most conducive to great jazz playing sometimes.
There’s not as much interaction between the audience so it’s hard for the musicians to get feedback, or energy from an audience. It’s kind of out there beyond the footlights I think.
I think so. Not everyone agrees, but I think yeah, I would agree with what you’re saying.
